concepts.statement: The linear hypothesis assumes that the risk of a radiation-induced cancer is proportional to the dose, even at doses too low for any effect to be observed. Scaling down from high doses in this way gives about $10/10^{6}\;\text{rem}\cdot\text{y}$ for the risk of cancer.

concepts.name: Background radiation
concepts.statement: Everyone receives background radiation, about 3 mSv a year on average, from cosmic rays, from rocks and soil, from the body's own nuclides and, above all, from radon. Its size varies from place to place and is the natural yardstick for every other dose.

concepts.name: Radiation protection
concepts.statement: A dose is limited in only three ways: by keeping the time of exposure short, by increasing the distance from the source and by placing shielding between the source and the body.

concepts.name: Rad
concepts.statement: The rad, short for radiation absorbed dose, is the dose that deposits 0.01 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue.

concepts.name: Gray
concepts.statement: The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, the dose that deposits 1 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue; one gray is 100 rad.

concepts.name: Rem
concepts.statement: The rem, short for roentgen equivalent man, is the unit of dose equivalent that goes with the rad: a dose in rad times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in rem.

concepts.name: Sievert
concepts.statement: The sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent: a dose in grays times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in sieverts, and one sievert is 100 rem.

concepts.name: Low dose
concepts.statement: A low dose is a dose of less than about 0.1 Sv (10 rem), below which no immediate effect can be observed.

concepts.name: Moderate dose
concepts.statement: A moderate dose is a dose from about 0.1 Sv to 1 Sv (10 to 100 rem), which can cause measurable changes in the blood and, near the top of the range, radiation sickness.

concepts.name: High dose
concepts.statement: A high dose is a dose greater than about 1 Sv (100 rem), which causes radiation sickness and, at several sieverts, can be fatal.

concepts.name: Hormesis
concepts.statement: Hormesis is the proposal that a very low dose of radiation may be beneficial, stimulating the body's repair mechanisms; the evidence for it is not conclusive.

concepts.name: Shielding
concepts.statement: Shielding is a layer of material placed between a radiation source and the body to absorb the radiation and so reduce the dose.

concepts.name: Therapeutic ratio
concepts.statement: Radiotherapy works because cancer cells, reproducing rapidly, are more sensitive to radiation than normal cells. Every technique aims to kill as many abnormal cells as possible for each normal cell killed.

concepts.name: Crossfire beams
concepts.statement: A single beam would give healthy tissue on its path the same dose as the tumor. Rotating the source about a point in the tumor keeps the dose high at the crossing point and spreads it thin everywhere else.

concepts.name: Therapeutic doses
concepts.statement: Doses of tens of sieverts would kill if given to the whole body at once. Localization and fractionation make them survivable, and the tolerable dose depends on the surrounding tissue.

concepts.name: Radiotherapy
concepts.statement: Radiotherapy is the use of ionizing radiation to treat disease, above all to destroy cancer cells.

concepts.name: Food irradiation
concepts.statement: Food irradiation is the treatment of food with ionizing radiation. It reduces pest infestation, delays spoilage and prevents illness caused by microorganisms, and because insects and bacteria tolerate far more radiation than people, it takes doses of thousands of grays.

concepts.name: No residual radioactivity in irradiated food
concepts.statement: The first worry about irradiated food is that it becomes radioactive. It does not, because $\gamma$ rays, x-rays and electrons at these energies induce no nuclear reactions.

concepts.name: Free radicals and radiolytic products
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation makes free radicals in food and in organisms, and their reactions produce new compounds called radiolytic products. Free radicals are how irradiation kills organisms, and the radiolytic products are the center of the debate about the safety of irradiated food.

concepts.name: Free radicals
concepts.statement: Free radicals are molecules or atoms with an unpaired electron, made when ionizing radiation breaks molecular bonds; they are highly reactive.

concepts.name: Radiolytic products
concepts.statement: Radiolytic products are the compounds produced in food by the chemical reactions of free radicals that irradiation creates.

concepts.name: Energy from fusion
concepts.statement: The binding energy per nucleon curve of Chapter 31 predicts both fusion and fission. Where two light nuclei make one with greater BE/$A$, mass is destroyed and energy released.

concepts.name: Coulomb barrier
concepts.statement: Two positive nuclei repel each other until they come close enough for the short-ranged nuclear attraction to take over. Their potential energy is therefore a hill, the Coulomb barrier, with a deep well at its center.

concepts.name: Fusion by tunneling
concepts.statement: The core of the Sun is too cool for nuclei to touch, yet it fuses hydrogen. Tunneling explains it, and because tunneling is so sensitive to how high up the barrier the nuclei climb, temperature controls the rate.

concepts.name: Proton-proton cycle
concepts.statement: The Sun shines by the proton-proton cycle, three reactions in which four protons and two electrons become a helium nucleus, two neutrinos and six $\gamma$ rays: $2e^{-} + 4\,{}^{1}\text{H} \to {}^{4}\text{He} + 2v_{\text{e}} + 6\gamma$, releasing 26.7 MeV. The first two reactions must happen twice for each helium nucleus made.

concepts.name: Solar neutrinos
concepts.statement: Energy from the core takes tens of thousands of years to reach the surface, but neutrinos leave in seconds. That makes them the only direct messengers from the reactions, and their shortfall led to the discovery that neutrinos have mass.

concepts.name: Deuterium-tritium fusion
concepts.statement: The proton-proton cycle is far too slow for a power plant. Reactions of deuterium and tritium are easier to induce, give large energies, and use a fuel that is plentiful in sea water.

concepts.name: Finding fusion energy from a mass of fuel
concepts.statement: The energy from fusing a given mass of fuel is the number of reactions in that mass times the energy per reaction, and dividing the energy by the time over which it is released gives the average power.

concepts.name: Break-even and ignition
concepts.statement: Practical fusion needs a hot enough fuel, dense enough, held together long enough; the three trade off against one another. Break-even and ignition are the milestones a reactor must pass.

concepts.name: Magnetic and inertial confinement
concepts.statement: Magnetic confinement holds a hot, thin plasma for a long time in a magnetic field, as in a tokamak, while inertial confinement compresses a dense fuel pellet with laser beams for a very short time. The two techniques trade density against confinement time.

concepts.name: Nuclear fusion
concepts.statement: Nuclear fusion is a reaction in which two nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus.

concepts.name: Break-even
concepts.statement: Break-even is the point at which a fusion reactor produces as much energy from fusion as is put into heating and confining its fuel.

concepts.name: Ignition
concepts.statement: Ignition is the point at which the fusion in a reactor produces enough energy to keep the fuel hot and fusing without any further energy put in.

concepts.name: Magnetic confinement
concepts.statement: Magnetic confinement is the technique of holding a hot fusion plasma away from the walls of its container with magnetic fields, as in a tokamak.

concepts.name: Inertial confinement
concepts.statement: Inertial confinement is the technique of compressing and heating a small pellet of fusion fuel so quickly, usually with laser beams, that it fuses before its own inertia lets it fly apart.

concepts.name: Energy from fission
concepts.statement: Fission is the other side of the binding energy curve. Reading about 7.6 MeV per nucleon near $A = 240$ against 8.6 near $A = 120$ estimates the energy of one fission, about 200 MeV, ten times a fusion and a hundred times a decay.

concepts.name: Calculating fission energy
concepts.statement: The energy released by a fission is the mass destroyed times $c^{2}$, found from the atomic masses of the reactants and of the products, with the neutrons counted among the products.

concepts.name: Neutron-induced fission
concepts.statement: In neutron-induced fission a neutron, having no charge, enters a heavy nucleus at low energy and deposits enough energy to set it oscillating like a struck drop until Coulomb repulsion splits it into two fragments and a few neutrons: $n + {}^{A}\text{X} \to \text{FF}_{1} + \text{FF}_{2} + xn$.

concepts.name: Chain reaction
concepts.statement: Because fission makes neutrons that can cause more fission, a chain reaction is possible when more than one neutron per fission goes on to fission another nucleus. How much material that takes is the critical mass, the central quantity of both reactors and bombs.

concepts.name: Fission of odd-neutron nuclei
concepts.statement: Why ${}^{235}\text{U}$ and ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ and not the plentiful ${}^{238}\text{U}$? The nuclear force is more attractive when the captured neutron makes the number even, so about 2 MeV more is deposited and the drop deforms further.

concepts.name: Reactor moderation and control
concepts.statement: ${}^{235}\text{U}$ captures slow neutrons best while fission gives fast ones, so a reactor needs a moderator; control rods keep it at criticality. The water also makes a safety feature, since losing it stops the chain reaction.

concepts.name: Finding fission energy from a mass of fuel
concepts.statement: The energy from fissioning a given mass of fuel is the number of nuclei in that mass times the energy per fission. Each fission gives ten times the energy of a fusion, but a kilogram of fission fuel gives only about a quarter as much as a kilogram of fusion fuel, because it holds far fewer nuclei.

concepts.name: Breeding plutonium
concepts.statement: Breeding turns ${}^{238}\text{U}$ into fissile ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$: the ${}^{238}\text{U}$ captures a neutron, and the ${}^{239}\text{U}$ formed decays by two $\beta^{-}$ decays through ${}^{239}\text{Np}$. Breeding makes the other 99 percent of natural uranium usable, and it makes bomb material.

concepts.name: Nuclear fission
concepts.statement: Nuclear fission is a reaction in which a nucleus splits into two or more smaller nuclei.

concepts.name: Fission fragments
concepts.statement: The fission fragments are the two daughter nuclei into which a nucleus splits in fission.

concepts.name: Liquid drop model
concepts.statement: The liquid drop model treats a nucleus as a drop of nuclear matter: energy deposited in it sets it oscillating and deforming, and when it deforms far enough the Coulomb repulsion of its two ends overcomes the short-ranged nuclear attraction and it splits.

concepts.name: Critical mass
concepts.statement: The critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material needed for a self-sustained chain reaction.

concepts.name: Criticality
concepts.statement: Criticality is the condition in which, on average, exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction proceeds at a steady rate.

concepts.name: Supercriticality
concepts.statement: Supercriticality is the condition in which, on average, more than one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction grows.

concepts.name: Breeder reactor
concepts.statement: A breeder reactor is a reactor designed to make more fissile fuel, such as ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ from ${}^{238}\text{U}$, than it consumes.

concepts.name: Fission bomb
concepts.statement: A bomb must hold a supercritical mass together for microseconds before it blows itself apart. The two designs differ in how fast they assemble it, which is why plutonium needed the implosion.

concepts.name: Thermonuclear bomb
concepts.statement: Fusion gives more energy per kilogram, and fast neutrons aid it, so almost nothing limits the size of a fusion bomb. The fission trigger makes tritium and heats the fuel.

concepts.name: Nuclear weapon yield
concepts.statement: The yield of a nuclear weapon is stated in kilotons or megatons of TNT and corresponds to a mass destroyed of a few grams to a few kilograms. Its energy goes into blast, thermal radiation and nuclear radiation in proportions unlike those of a conventional explosive.

concepts.name: Exchange of virtual particles
concepts.statement: A force is carried by the exchange of virtual particles, created for a short time in temporary violation of the conservation of mass-energy, as the uncertainty principle allows. Such a particle cannot be observed directly, because observing it would take more time than it exists.

concepts.name: Range and carrier mass
concepts.statement: A carrier particle can travel only as far as light goes in the time it may exist, $d \approx c\,\Delta t$, and that time is shorter the greater its mass. The heavier the carrier, the shorter the range of the force it carries.

concepts.name: Estimating a carrier mass
concepts.statement: The mass of a carrier particle is estimated from the range of its force in three steps: the range gives the time the particle may exist, the uncertainty principle turns that time into an energy, and $\Delta E = mc^{2}$ turns the energy into a mass. The same chain runs backward from a mass to a range.

concepts.name: Pions and muons
concepts.statement: The pions, discovered with about the mass Yukawa predicted, carry the strong force between nucleons; the muon, of nearly the same mass, does not feel the strong force at all.

concepts.name: Virtual particle
concepts.statement: A virtual particle is a particle created for a short time in temporary violation of the conservation of mass-energy, as the uncertainty principle allows, and which cannot be observed directly.

concepts.name: Pion
concepts.statement: A pion is the particle exchanged between nucleons that carries the strong nuclear force; it is a meson with a mass about 270 times the electron's.

concepts.name: Meson
concepts.statement: A meson is a particle whose mass is intermediate between the electron and nucleon masses, as the masses of the pions are; the name now covers an entire class of particles.

concepts.name: Properties of the four forces
concepts.statement: The four basic forces differ greatly in strength and range: gravity and the electromagnetic force have infinite range, the weak and strong nuclear forces are short ranged, and each is carried by its own particle, the graviton, the photon, the $W^{\pm}$ and $Z^{0}$, and the gluons.

concepts.name: Feynman diagram
concepts.statement: A Feynman diagram is a graph of time against position that shows particles approaching, exchanging virtual particles and leaving.

concepts.name: Quantum electrodynamics
concepts.statement: Quantum electrodynamics is the quantum theory of the electromagnetic force, which it treats as carried by virtual photons and calculates from Feynman diagrams. Every later theory of a force is modeled on it.

concepts.name: Carrier mass and force range
concepts.statement: The four ranges in Table 33.1 follow from one rule: the photon and graviton are massless, so their forces reach any distance, while the $W^{\pm}$ and $Z^{0}$, about 1000 times the pion's mass, give the weak force about 1/1000 of the strong force's range.

concepts.name: Gluon
concepts.statement: A gluon is one of eight massless particles that carry the strong force between quarks.

concepts.name: Creation of matter in accelerators
concepts.statement: A collision can create new particles from its energy, $m = \Delta E/c^{2}$, so the more energy an accelerator gives its particles, the heavier the particles it can create, within the conservation laws.

concepts.name: Early accelerators
concepts.statement: The first accelerators were the electrostatic Van de Graaff, which gives particles the energy of a single large voltage, and the cyclotron, which accelerates them across a gap with an alternating voltage of fixed frequency while a magnetic field bends them round again in ever larger circles.

concepts.name: Synchrotron
concepts.statement: A synchrotron is a circular accelerator in which the frequency of the accelerating voltage and the strength of the magnetic field rise as the particles gain energy, so that they keep to an orbit of fixed radius.

concepts.name: Synchrotron radiation
concepts.statement: Synchrotron radiation is the electromagnetic radiation given off by charged particles as a magnetic field bends their path. It costs light particles such as electrons the most energy.

concepts.name: Colliding beams
concepts.statement: A beam striking a fixed target must leave its products recoiling, wasting energy; two beams meeting head-on have zero total momentum, so particles of twice the beam energy can be made.

concepts.name: Finding energy gained across accelerating gaps
concepts.statement: The energy a particle gains across an accelerating gap is $\text{PE}_{\text{elec}} = qV$, so a proton gains 1 eV for each volt it crosses and the energy from a linear accelerator is the sum of its gap voltages.

concepts.name: Van de Graaff accelerator
concepts.statement: A Van de Graaff is an electrostatic accelerator that gives charged particles the energy of the single large voltage it builds up on a charged dome.

concepts.name: Cyclotron
concepts.statement: A cyclotron is an accelerator in which a magnetic field bends charged particles in a spiral while an alternating voltage of fixed frequency accelerates them each time they cross the gap between two hollow D-shaped electrodes.

concepts.name: Linear accelerator
concepts.statement: A linear accelerator accelerates charged particles in a straight line through a series of tubes, giving them energy across the gap between each tube and the next.

concepts.name: Antiparticles and annihilation
concepts.statement: Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and the opposite charge, and a particle and its antiparticle can annihilate, turning their whole mass into photons that move apart to keep the total momentum zero.

concepts.name: Hadrons and leptons
concepts.statement: Particles are classified first by the forces they feel: hadrons feel the strong nuclear force and leptons do not. Only six leptons exist and they seem fundamental, while the hadrons are many.

concepts.name: Bosons and fermions
concepts.statement: Particles are divided by spin into bosons, with integral spin, and fermions, with half-integral spin, which obey the exclusion principle. All carrier particles are bosons, while quarks and leptons are fermions.

concepts.name: Conservation of lepton family numbers
concepts.statement: The six leptons fall into three families, the electron, muon and tau families, and in every reaction the total electron family number $L_{e}$, muon family number $L_{\mu}$ and tau family number $L_{\tau}$ are each conserved.

concepts.name: Mesons and baryons
concepts.statement: The hadrons are of two kinds, told apart not by mass but by decay: a meson can decay to leptons and leave no hadron, while a baryon always decays to another baryon.

concepts.name: Conservation of baryon number
concepts.statement: In every reaction the total baryon number is conserved. This is why the proton, the lightest baryon, does not decay, and why the number of nucleons in a nuclear reaction stays the same.

concepts.name: Particle lifetime and force
concepts.statement: The stronger the force that causes a decay, the faster the decay, so a particle's lifetime shows which force is at work: about $10^{-23}$ s for the strong force and $10^{-10}$ s or longer for the weak force. Leptons among the products also point to the weak force.

concepts.name: Strangeness
concepts.statement: Strangeness $S$ is a quantum number given to particles to account for decays that every other conservation law allows but that never happen; it is 0 for the ordinary hadrons and nonzero for the strange particles.

concepts.name: Checking conservation in a decay
concepts.statement: A decay is checked by adding up the charge, baryon number, lepton family numbers and strangeness before and after: a decay that conserves all of them can happen, and one that changes strangeness can happen only through the weak force.

concepts.name: Boson
concepts.statement: A boson is a particle with integral spin, 0, 1, 2 and so on; bosons do not obey the Pauli exclusion principle.

concepts.name: Fermion
concepts.statement: A fermion is a particle with half-integral spin, 1/2, 3/2 and so on; fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle.

concepts.name: Hadron
concepts.statement: A hadron is a particle that feels the strong nuclear force.

concepts.name: Lepton
concepts.statement: A lepton is a fundamental particle that does not feel the strong nuclear force; the six leptons are the electron, muon and tau and their three neutrinos.

concepts.name: Baryon
concepts.statement: A baryon is a hadron that always decays to another baryon; it is made of three quarks.

concepts.name: Baryon number
concepts.statement: Baryon number $B$ is a quantum number equal to $+1$ for a baryon, $-1$ for an antibaryon and 0 for mesons and leptons.

concepts.name: Electron family number
concepts.statement: The electron family number $L_{e}$ is $+1$ for the electron and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles and 0 for every other particle.

concepts.name: Muon family number
concepts.statement: The muon family number $L_{\mu}$ is $+1$ for the muon and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles and 0 for every other particle.

concepts.name: Tau family number
concepts.statement: The tau family number $L_{\tau}$ is $+1$ for the tau and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles and 0 for every other particle.

concepts.name: Conservation of muon family number
terms: conservation of total muon family number
concepts.statement: In every reaction the total muon family number is conserved.

concepts.name: Conservation of strangeness
concepts.statement: Strangeness is conserved in reactions caused by the strong and electromagnetic forces but can change in reactions caused by the weak force.

concepts.name: Fundamental particles
concepts.statement: A fundamental particle is one with no substructure and no size beyond its wavelength. The known fundamental particles are of three types: the leptons, the quarks and the carrier particles.

concepts.name: Quark flavors
concepts.statement: The flavors are the six kinds of quark: up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top. Their charges are fractions of the proton's, $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ for the up, charm and top quarks and $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ for the down, strange and bottom quarks.

concepts.name: Quark composition of hadrons
concepts.statement: In the quark model every baryon is made of three quarks and every meson of a quark and an antiquark, rules that give hadrons only integral charges.

concepts.name: Finding quantum numbers from quarks
concepts.statement: A hadron's charge, baryon number and strangeness are found by adding those of its quarks, and working backward names the quarks of a particle from its quantum numbers.

concepts.name: Change of quark flavor
concepts.statement: The weak force can change the flavor of a quark, and the strong force cannot. Neutron decay is a down quark becoming an up quark, and the same change is why only the weak force can change strangeness.

concepts.name: Evidence for quarks
concepts.statement: No quark has been isolated, yet the evidence for quarks is strong: the $\Omega^{-}$ was found as the quark model predicted, high-energy electrons scatter from three pointlike charges inside the proton, and collisions produce jets of particles from single quarks.

concepts.name: Quark color and confinement
concepts.statement: Each quark carries one of three colors, and hadrons are always white, a baryon combining three colors and a meson a color and its anticolor. Color lets quarks in states such as $sss$ obey the exclusion principle and explains why a single quark cannot be isolated.

concepts.name: Three families
concepts.statement: Leptons, quarks and carrier particles each fall into three analogous families, normal, exotic and more exotic, and the particles of the higher families decay into those of the first.

concepts.name: Up quark
concepts.statement: The up quark is the quark flavor of charge $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ in the first family; the proton is $uud$.

concepts.name: Down quark
concepts.statement: The down quark is the quark flavor of charge $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ in the first family; the neutron is $udd$.

concepts.name: Strange quark
concepts.statement: The strange quark is the quark flavor of charge $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ and strangeness $-1$ in the second family.

concepts.name: Charm quark
concepts.statement: The charm quark is the quark flavor of charge $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ in the second family.

concepts.name: Bottom quark
concepts.statement: The bottom quark is the quark flavor of charge $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ in the third family.

concepts.name: Top quark
concepts.statement: The top quark is the quark flavor of charge $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ in the third family, by far the heaviest quark.

concepts.name: Color
concepts.statement: Color is a quantum number of quarks, with three values called red, green and blue, and their anticolors for antiquarks; it has nothing to do with visible color.

concepts.name: Quark confinement
concepts.statement: The theory of quark confinement holds that the force between quarks grows with their separation, so a single quark can never be isolated and quarks are found only in white combinations.

concepts.name: Quantum chromodynamics
concepts.statement: Quantum chromodynamics is the theory of the strong force between quarks, carried by gluons and acting on the quarks' color.

concepts.name: Electroweak theory
concepts.statement: Electroweak theory unifies the electromagnetic and weak forces, showing them to be one force at high energy. It predicted the $W^{\pm}$ and $Z^{0}$ and their masses before they were found.

concepts.name: Gluons and color
concepts.statement: Eight gluons carry the strong force between quarks and can change their color. Pion exchange between nucleons is, underneath, the exchange of quarks and gluons.

concepts.name: Standard Model
concepts.statement: The Standard Model is the combination of electroweak theory and quantum chromodynamics, the present theory of the fundamental particles and forces, with the Higgs boson its last predicted piece.

concepts.name: Grand Unified Theories
concepts.statement: A grand unified theory unifies the strong force with the electroweak force. Higher energy probes smaller distances, and at extremely high energies the strengths of the forces come together, far beyond the reach of any accelerator.

concepts.name: Proton decay
concepts.statement: Grand unified theories predict that the proton decays, as in $p \to \pi^{0} + e^{+}$, with a lifetime near $10^{31}$ y. Proton decay has not been observed, which constrains the theories.

concepts.name: Higgs boson
concepts.statement: The Higgs boson is a massive particle predicted by the Standard Model to explain why the other particles have mass, and found in 2012.

concepts.name: Look-back time
concepts.statement: Light from a distant galaxy has been on its way for as many years as the galaxy is light years away, so the farther we look, the older the universe we see.

concepts.name: Cosmological red shift
concepts.statement: The cosmological red shift is the stretching of the wavelength of light by the expansion of space while the light travels. Nearly every galaxy shows a red shift proportional to its distance; it is not a Doppler shift, and every observer sees the other galaxies receding.

concepts.name: Hubble’s law
concepts.statement: The recession velocity of a galaxy is proportional to its distance, $v = H_{0}d$, where the constant of proportionality $H_{0}$ is the Hubble constant.

concepts.name: Finding recession speed and distance
concepts.statement: Hubble's law turns a galaxy's distance into its recession speed and a recession speed, measured from a red shift, into a distance. The same arithmetic gives a rough age of the universe.

concepts.name: Cosmic microwave background
concepts.statement: The cosmic microwave background is blackbody radiation at about 2.7 K that fills all of space, the remnant of the hot early universe stretched to long wavelengths by its expansion. Its discovery is the second great piece of evidence for the Big Bang.

concepts.name: Matter-antimatter asymmetry
concepts.statement: The universe is nearly pure matter, although particle physics is almost symmetric between matter and antimatter. A tiny asymmetry of the forces in the early universe left a little matter over when the rest annihilated.

concepts.name: Wrinkles in the cosmic microwave background
concepts.statement: The cosmic microwave background shows tiny variations, or wrinkles, from one direction to another. Galaxies could not have formed without such early fluctuations in density, and yet the background is so smooth that its smoothness needs an explanation.

concepts.name: Epochs of the early universe
concepts.statement: Going back in time, the universe grows hotter and denser until the average particle energy reaches the energies at which the forces unify. The TOE, GUT and electroweak epochs are named for those unifications.

concepts.name: Symmetry breaking and inflation
concepts.statement: When the strong force separated from the electroweak force, the transition released energy that may have expanded the universe by a factor of $10^{50}$ or more in an instant. That inflation would stretch the early wrinkles nearly flat and so explain the smoothness of the background radiation.

concepts.name: Cosmology
concepts.statement: Cosmology is the study of the character and evolution of the universe.

concepts.name: Big Bang
concepts.statement: The Big Bang is the hot, dense beginning from which the universe has been expanding ever since, about 14 billion years ago.

concepts.name: Hubble constant
concepts.statement: The Hubble constant $H_{0}$ is the ratio of a galaxy's recession velocity to its distance, the slope of a graph of one against the other, about 20 (km/s)/Mly.

concepts.name: Superforce
concepts.statement: The superforce is the single unified force that the four basic forces are thought to have been at the highest energies of the early universe.

concepts.name: TOE epoch
concepts.statement: The TOE epoch is the time before about $10^{-43}$ s after the Big Bang, when all four forces were unified in the superforce.

concepts.name: GUT epoch
concepts.statement: The GUT epoch is the time after gravity separated, when the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces were still unified, ending about $10^{-35}$ s after the Big Bang.

concepts.name: Electroweak epoch
concepts.statement: The electroweak epoch is the time after the strong force separated, when the weak and electromagnetic forces were still unified, ending about $10^{-11}$ s after the Big Bang.

concepts.name: Spontaneous symmetry breaking
concepts.statement: Spontaneous symmetry breaking is the separation of a unified force into distinct forces as the universe cools, a transition that releases energy, as water releases energy when it freezes.

concepts.name: Inflationary scenario
concepts.statement: The inflationary scenario holds that the energy released when the strong force separated from the electroweak force expanded the universe by a factor of $10^{50}$ or more in an instant, stretching the early wrinkles nearly flat.

concepts.name: Equivalence of acceleration and gravity
concepts.statement: A person in a closed elevator cannot tell whether it accelerates upward or stands in a gravitational field. Einstein took this to hold in all situations, and general relativity grows from it.

concepts.name: Bending of light by gravity
concepts.statement: Light has no mass, yet its path bends in a gravitational field, because mass curves space and light follows the curve. Its observation in the 1919 eclipse was the first verification of general relativity.

concepts.name: Gravitational lensing
concepts.statement: Gravitational lensing is the bending of light from a distant galaxy by the gravity of a nearer one, which acts like a converging lens and can form several images. It is a large-scale test of general relativity.

concepts.name: Black holes and the event horizon
concepts.statement: An object whose escape velocity exceeds the speed of light lets nothing out. The event horizon is the distance at which the escape velocity is exactly the speed of light, and it is the edge of the black hole.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.statement: The radius of the event horizon of a black hole is $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$, in proportion to its mass. Since $G$ is small and $c^{2}$ is large, a black hole of a few solar masses is only a few kilometers across.

concepts.name: Finding a Schwarzschild radius
concepts.statement: The Schwarzschild radius $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$ turns the mass of a black hole into the size of its event horizon, from a stellar black hole to a supermassive one at a galaxy's core.

concepts.name: Neutron star
concepts.statement: In a supernova the core's electrons and protons are forced together into neutrons, and the strong force halts the collapse at a star of nuclear density. A neutron star is slightly larger than a black hole of the same mass.

concepts.name: Gravitational waves
concepts.statement: Gravitational waves are ripples in the curvature of space itself, sent out by moving masses as a water bug's foot sends waves across a pond. They travel at the speed of light and only extreme events make them strong enough to detect.

concepts.name: Black hole radiation
concepts.statement: Where gravity is strong enough to act on the quantum scale, quantum mechanics and general relativity must be used together. A black hole can then radiate, as pairs created near its horizon split and one member escapes.

concepts.name: General relativity
concepts.statement: General relativity is Einstein's theory of gravitation, in which mass curves space and time and the curvature governs the motion of matter and light.

concepts.name: Thought experiment
concepts.statement: A thought experiment is an experiment carried out in the mind rather than with apparatus, to reason out what a theory implies.

concepts.name: Escape velocity
concepts.statement: The escape velocity of a body is the smallest speed an object must have at its surface to escape the body's gravity entirely.

concepts.name: Black hole
concepts.statement: A black hole is an object so dense that its escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.

concepts.name: Event horizon
concepts.statement: The event horizon is the distance from a black hole at which the escape velocity equals the speed of light; nothing inside it can get out.

concepts.name: Quasar
concepts.statement: A quasar is an extremely distant and luminous object, thought to be the center of a young galaxy powered by a supermassive black hole.

concepts.name: Quantum gravity
concepts.statement: Quantum gravity is the theory, not yet found, that would describe gravity where it is strong enough to act on the quantum scale, by joining quantum mechanics and general relativity.

concepts.name: Superstring theory
concepts.statement: Superstring theory is an attempt at a Theory of Everything, and so must contain quantum gravity. Its particles, the graviton among them, act like one-dimensional vibrating strings in a superspace whose extra dimensions curled up as the forces separated.

concepts.name: Smallest length and time
concepts.statement: Quantum gravity suggests that space and time are grainy, with no meaning to intervals shorter than some tiny finite size. Superstrings would sit at that limit, with no further substructure.

concepts.name: Flat rotation curve
concepts.statement: The orbital speed of the stars in a galaxy stays almost constant out to great distances from its center, instead of falling off as it would if the galaxy's mass were concentrated, like its luminous stars, near the center. This flat rotation curve is the first evidence for dark matter.

concepts.name: Dark matter
concepts.statement: Dark matter is matter that cannot be seen but whose gravity shows it is there; there is about ten times as much of it in the universe as there is luminous matter, and what it is remains unknown.

concepts.name: Critical density
concepts.statement: The critical density $\rho_{\text{c}} \approx 10^{-26}\;\text{kg/m}^{3}$ is the average density of the universe that would just halt its expansion in a universe with no cosmological constant, a few nucleons per cubic meter.

concepts.name: Open, closed and flat universes
concepts.statement: An open universe is negatively curved and expands forever, a closed one is positively curved and returns a traveler to the start, and a flat one lies between. Measurements show the universe is very close to flat.

concepts.name: MACHOs and microlensing
concepts.statement: MACHOs, small dark bodies in a galaxy's halo, would not block a star's light but would focus it as they pass in front of it, and the star would brighten in a characteristic manner. Searches for such microlensing test whether dark matter is ordinary matter.

concepts.name: Neutrino oscillations
concepts.statement: A neutrino can change from one flavor to another only if it has mass, since a massless neutrino travels at the speed of light and no time passes for it. Oscillations explain the missing solar neutrinos and could supply some of the dark matter.

concepts.name: WIMPs
concepts.statement: WIMPs are proposed weakly interacting massive particles, chargeless and of a completely new kind, that could make up dark matter. They would gather in halos rather than coalesce into spirals.

concepts.name: Cosmological constant
concepts.statement: The cosmological constant is a term in Einstein's equations of general relativity that acts as a repulsion causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate.

concepts.name: Negatively curved universe
concepts.statement: A negatively curved universe is an open one, curved like a saddle, in which the angles of a large triangle add to less than $180^{\circ}$ and the expansion continues forever.

concepts.name: Positively curved universe
concepts.statement: A positively curved universe is a closed one, curved like a sphere, in which the angles of a large triangle add to more than $180^{\circ}$ and a traveler going straight returns to the start.

concepts.name: Flat universe
concepts.statement: A flat universe has zero curvature, so that the angles of a triangle add to exactly $180^{\circ}$; it lies between an open and a closed universe.

concepts.name: MACHO
concepts.statement: MACHOs, massive compact halo objects, are dark bodies of ordinary matter, such as faint stars and planets, in a galaxy's halo, proposed as part of the dark matter.

concepts.name: Microlensing
concepts.statement: Microlensing is the brightening of a distant star when a small dark body passes in front of it and focuses its light by gravitational lensing.

concepts.name: Axion
concepts.statement: Axions are a proposed kind of light, weakly interacting particle that could make up some of the dark matter.

concepts.name: Neutralino
concepts.statement: Neutralinos are proposed neutral, weakly interacting massive particles predicted by some theories, candidates for the dark matter.

concepts.name: Complexity
concepts.statement: Complexity is the study of complex adaptive systems, those that obey the simple laws of physics yet can adapt, organize themselves and evolve.

concepts.name: Chaos
concepts.statement: Chaos is a system's extreme sensitivity to its initial conditions, so that a small change in where it starts changes its outcome tremendously and its long-term behavior cannot be predicted with precision.

concepts.name: Order in chaos
concepts.statement: There can be organization in chaos, and it can be quantified. Some chaotic systems settle into a stable self-organized form.

concepts.name: High-temperature superconductors
concepts.statement: High-temperature superconductors are ceramics, found since 1986, that superconduct above 77 K, the boiling point of cheap liquid nitrogen, which makes them economically interesting.

concepts.name: Flux exclusion by superconductors
concepts.statement: A superconductor keeps magnetic flux out and so repels a magnet. A magnet floating above a cooled sample is the evidence that it is superconducting.

concepts.name: Comparing superconductor cooling cost
concepts.statement: A superconducting wire pays only when cooling it costs less than the energy a normal wire loses to heat, a comparison made with the power dissipated in a resistance and the price of electric energy.

concepts.name: Reproducibility at the frontier
concepts.statement: A result at the frontier is accepted only when it can be reproduced or is of such quality that a single observation is meaningful. Reports of superconductors above 200 K have not passed that test.

concepts.name: Superconducting critical temperature
concepts.statement: The critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$ of a superconductor is the temperature at and below which it has zero resistivity.

concepts.name: Open questions at every scale
concepts.statement: The open questions of physics lie on three scales, the largest, the intermediate and the smallest, and each rests on physics already known.

concepts.name: Connection of small and large scales
concepts.statement: Many of the open questions of cosmology have answers in particle physics, and the reverse. The closure of the universe, for example, depends on the type and number of particles that may contribute to it.

concepts.name: Energy quantization
concepts.statement: A quantized system can have only certain energies and not a continuum of them, which would be like a car that could travel only at certain speeds. This was the first break with classical physics.

concepts.name: Blackbody radiation
concepts.statement: An ideal radiator, a blackbody, emits a spectrum whose shape depends only on its temperature, and that shape could not be explained by classical physics. It was the curve of intensity against wavelength that gave the first clue that the energies of atoms are quantized.

concepts.name: Planck’s quantized oscillator energy
concepts.statement: Planck found that the atoms and molecules of a blackbody, treated as oscillators, could have only the energies $E = (n + \frac{1}{2})hf$. With this one assumption he described the measured blackbody spectrum correctly, and Planck’s constant $h$ entered physics.

concepts.name: Quantum energy step
concepts.statement: An oscillator of frequency $f$ can gain or lose energy only in discrete steps of size $hf$, much as a person on a staircase can stand only on the steps. Because $h$ is so small, these steps are far too small to notice in a macroscopic system.

concepts.name: Correspondence principle
concepts.statement: In the classical limit of large, slow-moving objects, quantum mechanics gives the same results as classical physics. This is why quantization goes unnoticed in everyday life.

concepts.name: Quantized energies from atomic spectra
concepts.statement: A hot gas emits only certain wavelengths, a line spectrum, and if each emission carries an energy $\Delta E = hf$, the energies of the electrons in the emitting atoms must be quantized.

concepts.name: Quantized
concepts.statement: A physical quantity is quantized when it exists only with particular discrete values and not with every value in a continuum.

concepts.name: Blackbody
concepts.statement: A blackbody is an ideal radiator, one that can radiate equally well at all wavelengths.

concepts.name: Planck’s constant
concepts.statement: Planck’s constant $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s is the constant that sets the size of the quantum steps of energy; Planck found its value by fitting his theory to the measured blackbody spectrum.

concepts.name: Atomic spectra
concepts.statement: Atomic spectra are the electromagnetic emission from atoms and molecules, which for a hot gas consists of only certain wavelengths.

concepts.name: Photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: When light strikes a material it can eject electrons, and the energy of those electrons can be measured with a retarding voltage. The details of this simple experiment are what forced Einstein to treat light itself as quantized.

concepts.name: Photon energy
concepts.statement: Einstein proposed that EM radiation is itself made of quanta, photons, each with an energy $E = hf$ proportional to its frequency. This is a quantization of the radiation, not only of the oscillators that emit it.

concepts.name: Properties of the photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: A threshold frequency below which no electrons leave however intense the light, ejection without delay, a number of electrons that grows with intensity and a maximum kinetic energy that does not: each of these follows from one photon meeting one electron, and several contradict a simple wave.

concepts.name: Einstein’s photoelectric equation
concepts.statement: The photon gives all its energy to one electron; part of it breaks the electron away from the material and the rest becomes the electron’s kinetic energy. This one line explains the photoelectric effect quantitatively, and its graph against frequency has Planck’s constant as its slope.

concepts.name: Photoelectric threshold
concepts.statement: A photon whose energy is less than the binding energy cannot free an electron at all, so each material has a threshold frequency $f_0 = \text{BE}/h$, and a longest wavelength, below which no electrons are ejected.

concepts.name: Finding a photon’s energy from its wavelength
concepts.statement: We usually describe light by its wavelength, so you most often find the photon energy by combining $E = hf$ with $c = f\lambda$. With it you can compare any photon with the energies of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.statement: A photon is a quantum, or particle, of electromagnetic radiation.

concepts.name: Work function
concepts.statement: The binding energy, also called the work function, is the energy needed to eject an electron from a material.

concepts.name: Photon energies in electron volts
concepts.statement: On the scale of atoms the electron volt is the natural unit, and with $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}$ eV·s and $hc = 1240$ eV·nm a photon energy is found in one division.

concepts.name: Photon energy and radiation effects
concepts.statement: Because photons interact one at a time with individual atoms and molecules, what a kind of radiation can do depends on how the energy of one photon compares with molecular and atomic energies. This explains why UV sunburns and visible light does not, and why dyes fade in a particular order.

concepts.name: Ionizing photons
concepts.statement: A photon with more energy than the 10 to 1000 eV needed to ionize an atom can damage tissue on its own, so the high-frequency end of the spectrum is hazardous in a way the low-frequency end is not. The same energy makes these photons useful in medical imaging and cancer treatment.

concepts.name: Maximum x-ray photon energy
concepts.statement: An electron accelerated through a voltage $V$ gains an energy $qV$, and when it strikes the anode it can give all of it to a single photon. So an x-ray tube’s voltage in kilovolts is its highest photon energy in keV, which is how its penetrating power is adjusted.

concepts.name: X-ray tube spectrum
concepts.statement: The x-ray spectrum of a tube has two parts: a smooth distribution from electrons braking in the anode, and sharp peaks that belong to the anode material. The peaks, like the lines of atomic spectra, are one more sign that the energy levels of atoms are quantized.

concepts.name: Counting photons per second
concepts.statement: Power is energy per unit time, so dividing a source’s power by the energy of one photon gives the number of photons it emits each second. The enormous numbers that result show why individual photons go unnoticed in ordinary life.

concepts.name: Microwaves
concepts.statement: Microwaves are the band of electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about a millimeter to about a meter, below the infrared in photon energy.

concepts.name: Bremsstrahlung
concepts.statement: Bremsstrahlung, German for braking radiation, is the radiation produced when electrons are decelerated, as in the anode of an x-ray tube.

concepts.name: Characteristic x rays
concepts.statement: Characteristic x rays are x rays whose energies depend on the material they were produced in, appearing as sharp peaks in the spectrum of an x-ray tube.

concepts.name: Photon momentum
concepts.statement: Photons have no mass, yet they carry momentum, and a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ carries $p = h/\lambda$. This is why comet tails point away from the Sun and why a space sail could be pushed by sunlight.

concepts.name: Compton effect
concepts.statement: When an x-ray photon scatters from an electron, the two collide like particles, energy and momentum are both conserved, and the scattered photon leaves with less energy and a longer wavelength. This was among the earliest direct evidence that momentum is conserved in quantum mechanics.

concepts.name: Photon momentum and energy
concepts.statement: Setting the mass to zero in the relativistic relation between energy and momentum gives $E = pc$ for a photon, and with $E = hc/\lambda$ this is Compton’s $p = h/\lambda$ again. The two routes to the same momentum tie the chapter to special relativity.

concepts.name: Size of photon momentum
concepts.statement: Because $h$ is so small, the momentum of visible light is tiny, which is why mirrors do not recoil. It becomes important only for short-wavelength photons meeting light particles, as in Compton’s experiment, or for enormous numbers of photons with nothing to stop the recoil.

concepts.name: Applying momentum conservation to photons
concepts.statement: A photon absorbed gives its momentum to the absorber, and a photon reflected straight back gives twice its momentum. With these two facts you can find the recoil of a dust grain, a sail or a mirror.

concepts.name: Particle-wave duality of EM radiation
concepts.statement: Light shows interference, which is a property of waves, and it interacts as discrete photons, which is a property of particles. The duality is the name for having both, and the next question it raises is whether matter has it too.

concepts.name: Particle or wave in one observation
concepts.statement: The duality seems strange because the words wave and particle come from large objects, which never act like both. On the quantum level our observations reveal one set of properties or the other, but not both simultaneously.

concepts.name: De Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: De Broglie proposed that every particle, with mass or without, has a wavelength $h/p$. It is the same relation as the photon’s, now applied to matter, and it opened the era in which quantum mechanics was founded.

concepts.name: Wave effects and obstacle size
concepts.statement: A wave must meet an object about as large as its wavelength to show interference, and a macroscopic body has a wavelength far smaller than anything known. This is why a bowling ball never diffracts and why the wave nature of matter was first seen with electrons.

concepts.name: Electron diffraction
concepts.statement: Davisson and Germer, and independently G. P. Thomson, scattered electrons from crystals and found diffraction patterns exactly consistent with the de Broglie wavelength. Interference is the hallmark of a wave, so these patterns showed that electrons are waves as well as particles.

concepts.name: Finding an electron’s speed and energy from its wavelength
concepts.statement: With $p = mv$ for a nonrelativistic particle, the de Broglie wavelength gives the speed, $v = h/m\lambda$, and from it the kinetic energy. Check that the speed really is well below the speed of light.

concepts.name: Electron microscope
concepts.statement: Resolution is limited to about one wavelength, and electrons from a modest voltage have wavelengths far smaller than those of visible light. The transmission and scanning electron microscopes use this to see details as small as individual atoms.

concepts.name: Bragg equation
concepts.statement: Planes of atoms in a crystal act like the slits of a diffraction grating: electrons scattered from successive planes interfere constructively when the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths. The same relation applies to x rays.

concepts.name: Probability distribution
concepts.statement: Each electron arrives at a definite place that cannot be predicted, yet many of them together build up a wave’s diffraction pattern. What quantum mechanics predicts is the probability of finding the particle at each location.

concepts.name: Measurement affecting the system
concepts.statement: A single electron at a time still builds up a double-slit pattern, so each electron interferes with itself. But if the slit it passes through is determined, the pattern becomes a single-slit one: measurement affects the system being observed.

concepts.name: Position-momentum uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: A probe short enough in wavelength to locate a particle well carries a large momentum and disturbs the particle’s momentum, so the two cannot both be known exactly. The product of their uncertainties can never be smaller than $h/4\pi$.

concepts.name: Energy-time uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: Energy cannot be measured precisely in a short time, so a short-lived state has an uncertain energy. The spread in the decay energies of short-lived particles is used to find their lifetimes.

concepts.name: Finding a minimum uncertainty
concepts.statement: Using the equals sign in either form of the principle gives the smallest possible uncertainty, and $\Delta p = m\Delta v$ turns a momentum uncertainty into a velocity uncertainty. Compare the result with atomic energies to judge whether it matters.

concepts.name: Uncertainty for large objects
concepts.statement: Planck’s constant is so small that the limits the principle sets are far below anything that matters for a planet or a ball. This is the correspondence principle again, and it is why we never notice the uncertainty principle in everyday life.

concepts.name: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle sets a fundamental limit to the precision with which pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum or energy and time, can be measured together.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in position
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in position is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of a particle’s position.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in momentum
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in momentum is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of a particle’s momentum.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in energy
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in energy is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of energy.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in time
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in time is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of time, such as the lifetime of a state.

concepts.name: Particle-wave duality of all particles
concepts.statement: Every particle, massless like the photon or with mass like the electron, has a wavelength and behaves as a particle, and so do combinations of them such as nuclei, atoms and molecules. The duality is a universal attribute of nature, one more connection between matter and energy.

concepts.name: Classical limit of particle-wave duality
concepts.statement: A large combination of massive particles has a wave nature too small to observe, and a large combination of photons shows mostly wave behavior. This is why classical physics saw matter only as particles and light only as waves.

concepts.name: Solving an integrated photon problem
concepts.statement: A problem that joins photon energy and momentum to momentum conservation, heat transfer, circuits, wave optics or relativity is solved by identifying the physical principles involved and solving each part with the strategy of its own chapter.

concepts.name: 温度
concepts.statement: 温度在操作上被定义为用温度计测量的量。你对冷热的感觉是相对的：对于刚才放在热水里的手，温水感觉是凉的；对于刚才放在冷水里的手，温水感觉是暖的。放在同一水中的两支精确的温度计给出相同的读数。许多物理量只是由我们测量它们的方式来定义的，而在本章后面，温度获得了更偏物理的含义，它与原子和分子的动能相联系。

concepts.name: 温度计
concepts.statement: 任何依赖于温度、且对温度的响应可重复的物理性质，都可以作为温度计的基础。对大多数物质来说，体积随温度升高而增大，这是酒精温度计、水银温度计和双金属片的基础。电阻、颜色和红外辐射的发射同样可以用。由于有这么多性质依赖于温度，温度计的种类之多令人惊叹。

concepts.name: 温标
concepts.statement: 温标以两个易于复现的温度为起点，通常是水在标准大气压下的凝固点和沸点。摄氏温标把它们定为 0 °C 和 100 °C，华氏温标把它们定为 32 °F 和 212 °F，所以一摄氏度的大小是一华氏度的 1.8 倍。开尔文温标是科学上的热力学温标。它的零点是绝对零度，它的单位是开尔文，不带度的符号，一开尔文与一摄氏度大小相等，所以水在 273.15 K 凝固，在 373.15 K 沸腾。

concepts.name: 温标之间的温度换算
concepts.statement: 三种常用温标之间的温度换算用表 13.1 的方程进行。由摄氏温标换算到华氏温标是乘以五分之九再加 32，由摄氏温标换算到开尔文温标是加 273.15，而华氏温标与开尔文温标之间的换算看起来复杂，其实就是这两者的简单组合。温差的换算与温度的换算不同：摄氏度改变一度，就是开尔文改变一度，也是华氏度改变五分之九度，没有偏移量。

concepts.name: 绝对零度
concepts.statement: 绝对零度的概念来自气体的行为。保持体积不变的气体的压强，随温度降低而沿一条直线下降，不同气体的直线都外推到同一温度时压强为零，这个温度是 −273.15 °C。这表明存在一个最低温度，而其他热力学关系也导出同样的结论。在绝对零度 0 K 时，分子运动处于可能的最低能量；大多数气体在达到绝对零度之前就已液化然后凝固，而且实际上不可能达到绝对零度。

concepts.name: 热平衡
concepts.statement: 两个处于热接触的系统，当它们的温度相同时就处于热平衡，这时没有热量在它们之间流动，两者的温度也都不再变化。任何两个处于热接触、但与环境的其余部分隔绝的系统都会达到这种状态：热量从较热的物体流向较冷的物体，直到它们的温度相等。这就是为什么温度计（它实际测量的是它自己的温度）在经过足够长的时间之后，读出的是它所接触物体的温度。单个物体在其内部没有热量流动、温度均匀时，处于内部热平衡。

concepts.name: 热力学第零定律
concepts.statement: 如果系统 A 和 B 彼此处于热平衡，而 B 又与第三个系统 C 处于热平衡，那么 A 也与 C 处于热平衡。这个结论看似显而易见，因为三者具有相同的温度，但它是热力学的基础。它之所以称为第零定律，是因为它在逻辑上先于第一和第二定律，尽管物理学家是在它们之后才表述它的。它让你可以相信，分别接触同一块板上两个不同物块的两支温度计，读出的是同一个数，因此它使温度成为一个有意义的概念。

concepts.name: 摄氏温标
concepts.statement: 摄氏温标是这样一种温标：在标准大气压下，水的凝固点为 0 °C，沸点为 100 °C。

concepts.name: 摄氏度
concepts.statement: 摄氏度是摄氏温标的单位，为水的凝固点与沸点之间间隔的百分之一。它与开尔文大小相同。

concepts.name: 华氏温标
concepts.statement: 华氏温标是这样一种温标：在标准大气压下，水的凝固点为 32 °F，沸点为 212 °F。

concepts.name: 华氏度
concepts.statement: 华氏度是华氏温标的单位，为水的凝固点与沸点之间间隔的一百八十分之一，所以一摄氏度的大小是它的 1.8 倍。

concepts.name: 开尔文温标
concepts.statement: 开尔文温标是科学上的热力学温标。它的零点是绝对零度，它的单位开尔文写作 K，不带度的符号，与一摄氏度大小相等，所以水在 273.15 K 凝固，在 373.15 K 沸腾。

concepts.name: 热膨胀
concepts.statement: 热膨胀是给定质量的物体的大小或体积随温度的变化。热空气上升是由于热膨胀：膨胀的空气密度比周围的空气小，对给定质量的浮力更大；铁轨和桥需要伸缩缝也是由于它。其原因在于，温度升高使原子的动能增大，原子微小而快速的振动平均而言把相邻的原子推得稍远一些，这稍大一点的间距累积起来就成为更大的物体。对大多数物质来说，没有择优的方向，物体在每个维度上按相同的比例增大。

concepts.name: 线膨胀
concepts.statement: 物体长度的变化与其长度和温度的变化成正比，比例系数是线胀系数，它取决于材料，并随温度略有变化。由于一开尔文与一摄氏度大小相同，系数和温度变化都可以用其中任何一种。该方程对温度的小变化是精确的，对大的变化可以用线胀系数的平均值。

forms.condition: 温度的小变化

concepts.name: 二维热膨胀
concepts.statement: 物体在所有维度上都膨胀，所以面积增大，是因为它的长度和宽度都增大。对于小的温度变化，面积的变化等于线胀系数的两倍乘以面积再乘以温度的变化，因为两个维度各自贡献线性的比例。

forms.condition: 温度的小变化

concepts.name: 孔的膨胀
concepts.statement: 如果在一块金属板上切出一个孔，剩下的材料的膨胀恰如那块圆塞仍在原处时一样。圆塞会变大，所以孔也一定变大：孔壁上相邻的一圈原子随温度升高而相互推得更远，这一圈就变得稍大一些。加热一个物体时，孔不会闭合。

concepts.name: 三维热膨胀
concepts.statement: 体积的变化非常接近于线胀系数的三倍乘以体积再乘以温度变化。该方程通常使用约为线胀系数三倍的体胀系数，表 13.2 中的数值几乎精确地显示了这一点。液体和气体只有体胀系数，而气体的系数是所有系数中最大的，并且对每一种气体几乎相同。

concepts.name: 求膨胀的液体溢出多少
concepts.statement: 当装满的容器和其中的液体一起变暖时，两者都膨胀，但液体膨胀得更多，溢出的量是两者体积变化之差。由于原来的体积相等，三个方程合并成一个：溢出量等于两个体胀系数之差乘以体积再乘以温度变化。同样的差值，也是夏天油箱里的质量比冬天更少时油量表就显示为空的原因，也是装满到杯口的烧杯变暖时会溢出的原因。

concepts.name: 水的反常膨胀
concepts.statement: 水是物体随温度升高而膨胀这一规律的最重要的例外。在 4 °C 以上，它随温度升高而膨胀，但在 4 °C 和 0 °C 之间，它随温度降低而膨胀，所以它在 4 °C 时密度最大。最显著的效应是池塘的结冰：表面的水冷却到 4 °C，下沉，并使池塘的水上下翻转，直到整个池塘的水都处于 4 °C；表面一层进一步冷却后，密度比下面的水小而留在上面，于是表面结冰，冰使下面的水与外界隔热，鱼就在那里度过冬天。

concepts.name: 热应力
concepts.statement: 当有东西限制热膨胀或收缩时，就会产生热应力。要求一个受热物体若不能膨胀将会施加的压强，先取它在固定压强下会产生的体积变化，再用体积模量求出把这一体积挤回去所需的压强。这样的压强通常大得惊人：保持体积不变的汽油经历 20 °C 的升温，将达到 1.83 × 10⁷ Pa，约 2500 lb/in²，远远超出油箱所能承受的。热应力使铁轨弯曲，使输电线绷断，使冷却不均匀的玻璃开裂，使岩石和路面风化，也使食物冻结时的生物细胞胀破。

concepts.name: 线胀系数
concepts.statement: 线胀系数是每单位长度、温度每改变一度时长度的变化。它取决于材料，并随温度略有变化，它的单位是摄氏度的倒数，1/°C。

concepts.name: 体胀系数
concepts.statement: 体胀系数是每单位体积、温度每改变一度时体积的变化。对固体来说，它非常接近线胀系数的三倍，而液体的值比固体大得多。

concepts.name: 理想气体
concepts.statement: 气体中的原子和分子相互间隔与它们自身的大小相比相距很远，所以除了碰撞时，它们之间的力可以忽略，气体会膨胀到充满它所能到达的任何体积。这就是为什么气体的体胀系数最大、而且几乎全都相同，而液体和固体则相差很大：气体的性质取决于单位体积内有多少个分子以及温度，而不取决于分子的种类。粒子体积可以忽略、只通过完全弹性碰撞相互作用的气体称为理想气体，室温下的空气在大多数情况下都是理想气体。

concepts.name: 理想气体定律
concepts.statement: 理想气体定律通过玻尔兹曼常量，把气体的绝对压强、体积、其中的原子和分子数以及它的热力学温度联系起来。它是一个物态方程，即系统的热力学性质之间的一个关系。它最初来自实验：查理定律说，在压强一定时体积与温度成正比；玻意耳定律说，在温度一定时压强乘以体积是常量。它在大多数条件下描述实际气体，并且对任何气体或混合气体都成立，因为只有分子的总数进入方程。务必使用绝对压强和热力学温度。

concepts.name: 玻尔兹曼常量
concepts.statement: 把分子数和热力学温度换算为压强与体积之积的常量，是以路德维希·玻尔兹曼命名的玻尔兹曼常量，其值为 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K。它的单位说明了它的作用：它把能量与温度联系起来，所以 kT 是每个分子的能量。

concepts.name: 把理想气体定律用作比值
concepts.statement: 当气体改变状态而它的某些性质保持不变时，对初态写一次这个定律，对末态再写一次，然后用一个除以另一个。保持不变的量都约掉了，玻尔兹曼常量也约掉了，只剩下一个关于发生变化的量的关系。对于体积和其中所含的气体都不变的轮胎，末态压强与初态压强的比值等于末态热力学温度与初态热力学温度的比值，这就是温度必须用开尔文的原因。

forms.condition: 体积和分子数不变

concepts.name: 摩尔
concepts.statement: 摩尔是物质的量的 SI 单位，它很方便，因为任何普通物体中的分子数都极其庞大。一摩尔含有阿伏伽德罗常量个粒子，不论是什么物质，并且任何物质的一摩尔，其以克为单位的质量等于它的分子质量，这可以从元素周期表上读出。物质的量等于分子数除以阿伏伽德罗常量。

concepts.name: 阿伏伽德罗常量
concepts.statement: 阿伏伽德罗常量是一摩尔中的粒子数，取三位有效数字为每摩尔 6.02 × 10²³ 个。这是为纪念阿梅代奥·阿伏伽德罗，他正确地提出：在相同压强和温度下，相同体积的气体含有相同数目的分子。自 2019 年起，一摩尔恰好是 6.02214076 × 10²³ 个基本单元。这个数如此之大，以至于一摩尔乒乓球可以把地球覆盖到约 40 km 的深度。

concepts.name: 用物质的量表示的理想气体定律
concepts.statement: 将理想气体定律乘以并除以阿伏伽德罗常量，就把分子数变成了物质的量，把玻尔兹曼常量变成了摩尔气体常量。这个常量是阿伏伽德罗常量乘以玻尔兹曼常量：在 SI 单位制中是 8.31 J/(mol·K)，在其他单位制中是 1.99 cal/(mol·K) 或 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K)。使用与你已知量相匹配的定律形式，即分子数或物质的量，并使用与问题所用单位相匹配的气体常量的值。

concepts.name: 标准状况下的摩尔体积
concepts.statement: 标准状况是 0 °C 和大气压。在标准状况下，理想气体定律给出任何气体每立方米中有 2.68 × 10²⁵ 个分子，即每立方米 44.5 mol，每摩尔 22.5 L（在三位数字输入的精度范围内；公认值是 22.4 L/mol）。由于每种气体的数目相同，一立方米气体的质量仅由摩尔质量就可得出。摩尔质量为 28.8 g/mol 的干空气每立方米重 1.28 kg，所以一间客厅里约有 90 kg 的空气，相当于一个人的质量。

forms.condition: 在标准状况（0 °C、1 atm）下

concepts.name: 能量形式的理想气体定律
concepts.statement: 理想气体定律的两边都具有能量的量纲，在 SI 单位制中是焦耳。压强是单位面积上的力，所以压强乘以体积是力乘以位移，也就是功。右边与该温度下分子的平动动能成正比，下一节将会说明这一点。气体含有与它的压强和体积两者都有关的能量，而理想气体定律是能量守恒的另一种表达：给轮胎打气所做的功，用于产生空气的压强，并用于使打气筒和空气变暖。

concepts.name: 摩尔气体常量
concepts.statement: 摩尔气体常量是阿伏伽德罗常量与玻尔兹曼常量的乘积，R = 8.31 J/(mol·K)。它对一摩尔气体所起的作用，就像玻尔兹曼常量对单个分子所起的作用。

concepts.name: 气体动理论
concepts.statement: 气体动理论假设原子和分子处于持续的无规运动中，并由这个假设解释压强和温度。当分子与刚性器壁发生弹性碰撞时，它的动量垂直于器壁的分量反向，所以器壁对它施加一个力，并且根据牛顿第三定律，它也对器壁施加一个力。极大数目的分子在短时间内撞击器壁，我们观察到的是单位面积上的平均力。分子越多，碰撞越多，压强越大；分子越快，碰撞越猛，压强越大。

concepts.name: 由分子推出理想气体定律
concepts.statement: 跟踪盒子里的一个分子，就得到气体的压强。每次碰撞时，它的动量变化是其垂直动量的两倍，它与一面器壁相继两次碰撞的平均时间间隔，是穿过盒子再返回的时间，所以单个分子产生的平均力，等于它的质量乘以其垂直速率的平方再除以盒子的长度。乘以分子数，把垂直分量换成方均速率的三分之一（因为运动是无规的，三个方向相同），再除以器壁的面积，就得到压强。结果 PV = ⅓Nm v̄² 是理想气体定律的另一种表达，现在是用分子的质量和速率表示的。

concepts.name: 分子的热能
concepts.statement: 令理想气体定律的分子形式等于 PV = NkT 并整理，可知分子的平均平动动能等于玻尔兹曼常量与热力学温度之乘积的二分之三。这个平均动能就是热能。这个方程给出了温度的分子解释，对气体成立，对液体和固体也相当准确。它用分子运动的能量来定义温度，并且在给定温度下，对每一种分子都是相同的。

forms.condition: 单原子理想气体

concepts.name: 方均根速率
concepts.statement: 由热能方程解出速率，得到分子的方均根速率，即方均速率的平方根，它随热力学温度的平方根增大，随分子质量的平方根减小。它大得出奇，室温下氮气为 511 m/s，但它不产生风，因为分子向各个方向运动的情形相同，并且在两次碰撞之间只运动极小的平均自由程。声速在室温下约为 340 m/s，它反映了这一点，这就是为什么声音在热空气和氦这样的轻质气体中更快。

concepts.name: 求分子的质量
concepts.statement: 单个原子或分子的质量，等于摩尔质量（从元素周期表上读出，以克每摩尔为单位，再换算为千克）除以一摩尔中的粒子数。氮分子是两个 14.0067 g/mol 的原子，所以质量为 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg；氦原子为 6.65 × 10⁻²⁷ kg。每一次对方均根速率的计算，或由速率求温度的计算，都要经过这一步。

forms.latex: m = \frac{\text{摩尔质量}}{\text{每摩尔的原子数}}

concepts.name: 麦克斯韦-玻尔兹曼分布
concepts.statement: 任何一个分子的运动，其大小和方向都是无规的，但由许多分子组成的气体具有可以预测的速率分布，即麦克斯韦-玻尔兹曼分布，它由气体动理论算出，并为实验所证实。这个分布有一条长长的尾部，因为有少数分子的速率是方均根速率的几倍，而它的峰值，即最概然速率，低于方均根速率。随着温度升高，整个分布向较高的速率移动并变宽，这就是为什么发热的人会从口腔和肺的内壁损失更多的水分。

concepts.name: 轻质气体从大气中逃逸
concepts.statement: 要从大气顶部摆脱地球的引力，物体必须以 11.1 km/s 的速率运动，而氦需要约 2 × 10⁴ K 的温度，其方均根速率才能达到这个值。然而空气中的氦含量极少。原子的速率时时刻刻都在变化，而在任一时刻，分布尾部中的一小部分都超过逃逸速度；经过几十亿年，这一部分就逸散掉了。较重的分子，氧、氮和水，方均根速率较小，能达到逃逸速度的非常之少，所以地球保住了它的大气。月球的引力弱得多，它几乎失去了全部大气，它白天的天空是黑色的。

concepts.name: 实际气体的凝结
concepts.statement: 实际气体在高温时的行为像理想气体，但在较低温度时，分子之间的相互作用和分子本身的体积开始起作用。分子靠得很近，气体凝结，物质变成液体时体积骤然下降。进一步冷却变成固体，体积再略微缩小，但永远不会缩到零，因为分子本身有体积。高压也可以使气体液化，工业上就是这样制造液态二氧化碳和液氮的。

concepts.name: PV 图
concepts.statement: 压强对体积的图像是 PV 图。对于温度和分子数固定的理想气体，乘积 PV 是常量，所以每条等温线，即某一温度下的曲线，都是双曲线，上面的曲线对应更热的温度。在较低的温度下，这些曲线不再像双曲线，因为气体不再表现为理想气体，并且可能含有液体；沿着低温等温线的平直部分，压强保持不变而体积变化，因为物质正在发生相变。

forms.condition: 理想气体，温度和分子数不变

concepts.name: 临界点
concepts.statement: 在物质的临界温度以上，液相在任何压强下都不能存在。该温度的等温线是具有平直的两相部分的最高一条，在它之上，被压缩得足够厉害的气体可以达到液体的密度而不凝结。临界压强是液体在临界温度下存在所需的最小压强。二氧化碳在 31 °C 以上不能成为液体，氧在 −118 °C 以上也不能，所以无论怎样挤压都不能使氧在室温下液化。

concepts.name: 相图
concepts.statement: 压强对温度的图像是相图：其中有明确的区域，物质在这些区域里是固体、液体或气体，而区域之间的实线是两个相共存的温度和压强。对水来说，液体-蒸气曲线给出每个压强下的沸点，1.00 atm 时为 100 °C，218 atm 时升高到 374 °C，这就是为什么高压锅烹饪更快；固体-液体曲线给出熔点，对水来说它向一侧倾斜，使熔点随压强增大而降低，这就是为什么雪球能被压实，也是为什么轮胎会把雪熔化成一层冰。知道了压强和温度，你就可以从图上读出相。

concepts.name: 升华
concepts.statement: 在足够低的压强下，不存在液相，物质直接在固态和气态之间转变。从固态到气态的相变是升华；它解释了积雪没有汇入河流就消失的现象、冰箱的自动除霜以及冷冻干燥。对水来说，低于 0.00600 atm 时没有液体，而二氧化碳在通常的大气压下就升华，这就是为什么固态二氧化碳是干冰：它不熔化。

concepts.name: 三相点
concepts.statement: 相图的三条曲线交于一点，即三相点，固体、液体和气体在此同时处于平衡共存。对水来说，它在 273.16 K 和 0.00600 atm，由于它是单一的、明确的温度和压强，所以它作为校准温度，比 1.00 atm 下的熔点 273.15 K 更精确。每种物质都有一个三相点，表 13.4 列出了几种。

concepts.name: 相平衡
concepts.statement: 液体和气体在沸点下处于平衡。在密闭容器中，液体沸腾和气体凝结的速率相同，两者的量没有净变化，因为分子离开液体成为气体的速度，与气体分子附着于液体的速度一样快。在较高温度下，液体沸腾得更快，气体中的分子更多，气体压强更高，凝结加快到与之相当，所以这一对在新的压强下再次达到平衡。敞口锅中 100 °C 的水会沸腾蒸发殆尽，敞口杯中 20 °C 的水会蒸发，因为它们上方的气体是空气而不是纯水蒸气。低于其沸点的气体是蒸气。

concepts.name: 蒸气压
concepts.statement: 蒸气压是气体与其固相或液相共存时的压强。它由从液体或固体挣脱出来进入气体的较快的分子产生，所以它取决于物质及其温度，温度升高使它增大。当水的蒸气压超过周围气体中水蒸气的分压时，水蒸发，冰升华；小于时，则形成液滴或霜。

concepts.name: 道尔顿分压定律
concepts.statement: 气体的分压是它单独占据全部可用体积时所产生的压强，在气体混合物中，总压强等于各组分分压之和，假设气体表现为理想气体且不发生化学反应。这就是道尔顿分压定律，它可由气体动理论得出：每种气体靠自己的分子碰撞产生压强，与存在的其他气体无关，而压强相加正如帕斯卡原理所说。

concepts.name: 蒸气
concepts.statement: 蒸气是温度低于其物质沸点的气体，因此它可以与液体共存。

concepts.name: 分压
concepts.statement: 混合气体中一种气体的分压，是它单独占据全部可用体积时所产生的压强。

concepts.name: 临界温度
concepts.statement: 物质的临界温度是这样一个温度：高于它，无论压强多大，其液相都不能存在。

concepts.name: 临界压强
concepts.statement: 物质的临界压强是其液相在临界温度下存在所需的最小压强。

concepts.name: 相对湿度与饱和
concepts.statement: 相对湿度表明空气中的水蒸气相对于可能的最大量有多少。在最大量，即饱和时，相对湿度为 100%，蒸发受到抑制，我们感觉更热，因为汗不再使我们变凉。空气能够容纳的水蒸气量通过水的蒸气压而取决于温度：在 100% 湿度时，水蒸气的分压等于蒸气压，低于它则蒸发继续进行，高于它则发生凝结。水并不是由空气容纳的；空气中的水量仅由水的蒸气压决定，与空气的性质无关。

concepts.name: 求饱和蒸气密度
concepts.statement: 水蒸气的行为像理想气体。产生给定分压的蒸气的密度，可由 PV = nRT 解出每立方米的物质的量，再用水的摩尔质量 18.0 g/mol 换算成克得到。在 20.0 °C 时，2.33 × 10³ Pa 的蒸气压给出 17.2 g/m³，恰好是表 13.5 中的饱和蒸气密度。该表中的密度是每个温度下每立方米所能容纳的水蒸气的最大量。

concepts.name: 相对湿度百分比
concepts.statement: 相对湿度百分比是空气中实际的蒸气密度与该温度下的饱和蒸气密度之比乘以 100。借助表 13.5，它可以回答许多关于一天天气的问题：25.0 °C 且含有 9.40 g/m³ 的空气，相对湿度为 40.9%，而露点为 −10.0 °C 的同样的空气，相对湿度只有 10.3%。

forms.latex: \text{相对湿度百分比} = \frac{\text{蒸气密度}}{\text{饱和蒸气密度}}\times 100

concepts.name: 露点
concepts.statement: 露点是空气中的水蒸气达到饱和密度时的温度，这时相对湿度将为 100%。在该温度，水开始从空气中凝结出来，成为露、雾或霜。气温不能降到露点以下而不发生水的凝结，而凝结释放出可观的热量，使温度维持不降。这就是为什么农民要关注露点，为什么沙漠的夜晚如此寒冷，以及为什么雾会在傍晚降温时形成。

concepts.name: 由饱和表读出湿度
concepts.statement: 每个湿度问题都要用到表 13.5。空气中的蒸气密度、空气温度下的饱和密度和露点下的饱和密度，是同一列中的三个条目。湿度、蒸气密度、露点和温度中的任何一个，都可由其余几个得出。湿度是两个密度之比，露点是饱和密度等于空气中蒸气密度的那个温度，而空气冷却时凝结出的水是两个饱和密度之差。当温度落在两行之间时，进行内插。

concepts.name: 沸点与压强
concepts.statement: 水在 100 °C 沸腾，因为那是它的蒸气压达到 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa（一个大气压）的温度，这样它就能无限制地蒸发。气泡的形成是因为水中溶有空气：锅底的气泡含有空气和水蒸气，总压强为 1.00 atm，随着温度升高，其中的水蒸气增多，气泡膨胀以保持其压强；在 100 °C 时蒸气不断进入，气泡长大，它的浮力增大，于是脱离并上升。当水所受的压强不同，沸腾温度也不同：在高压锅里或在深处较高，在高海拔处和真空室里较低。

concepts.name: 蒸发使留下的物体变冷
concepts.statement: 我们在炎热的天气里靠皮肤上汗水的蒸发和呼吸道里水的蒸发来保持凉爽，而高湿度抑制这种蒸发，这就是潮湿的炎热更难受的原因。最可能从液体逸出的分子是速率最大的那些，所以留下的分子平均速率较低，温度也较低；降低周围的压强会降低水的分压，加快蒸发，并且可以使食物冷却到冻结，冷冻干燥机就是这样工作的。吹热风使头发干得更快，因为较高的温度提高了蒸发的速率。

concepts.name: 饱和
concepts.statement: 当空气的相对湿度为 100% 时，空气是饱和的，即它在该温度下所含的水蒸气已达最大量，水蒸气的分压等于水的蒸气压。

concepts.name: Radioactivity
concepts.statement: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of some nuclei, which destroys a small part of their mass and emits energetic rays from the nucleus.

concepts.name: Nuclear origin of radiation
concepts.statement: The rays of radioactivity come from the nucleus, not the electrons: they do not vary with chemical state, temperature, pressure or ionization, all of which affect electrons, and each event carries energies of the order of a million electron volts, far beyond atomic energies of a few eV.

concepts.name: Alpha, beta and gamma rays
concepts.statement: Physicists named the three kinds of nuclear radiation before anyone knew what they were. A magnetic field bends alphas and betas in opposite directions and leaves gammas alone, which shows their charges. Later work showed that an alpha is a helium nucleus, a beta is an electron created at the instant of decay, and a gamma is a high-energy photon from a nucleus.

concepts.name: Ionizing radiation
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation is radiation, whether nuclear in origin or not, that ionizes the material that absorbs it. Nuclear decays emit from a few keV to more than 10 MeV per event, while it takes only a few eV to ionize an atom, so the radiation damages tissue and electronics and can be detected.

concepts.name: Range of radiation
concepts.statement: The range of radiation is the distance it travels through a material. Higher energy gives a greater range, a material dense in electrons gives a smaller one, and at the same energy alphas stop first, betas go farther and gammas farthest, because a greater charge and a lower speed make a particle ionize more readily.

concepts.name: Nuclear radiation
concepts.statement: Nuclear radiation is the rays that originate in the nuclei of atoms, the first examples of which were discovered by Becquerel.

concepts.name: Radioactive
concepts.statement: A substance or object is radioactive when it emits nuclear radiation.

concepts.name: Alpha rays
concepts.statement: Alpha rays are the kind of nuclear radiation bent by a magnetic field as positive charges, later found to be helium nuclei.

concepts.name: Beta rays
concepts.statement: Beta rays are the kind of nuclear radiation bent by a magnetic field opposite to alpha rays, later found to be electrons created at the instant of decay.

concepts.name: Counting ion pairs
concepts.statement: The number of ion pairs a particle can create is the energy it deposits divided by the energy needed to create each pair, which connects the MeV energies of nuclear radiation to the tens of eV of an ionization.

concepts.name: Detection by ionization
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation cannot be sensed directly, and every radiation detector, from photographic film to a semiconductor, turns the ionization or excitation that radiation produces into something that can be seen or measured.

concepts.name: Geiger tube
concepts.statement: In a Geiger tube a voltage between a cylinder and a wire along its axis sweeps up the ion pairs that radiation creates in the gas, and the counter records the brief current as a count. A count does not give the energy, charge or type of the radiation.

concepts.name: Scintillators and photomultipliers
concepts.statement: A second family of detectors records light instead of charge. A scintillator converts the energy of radiation into brief flashes of light, and a photomultiplier multiplies the photoelectrons from each flash at a series of dynodes into a measurable current proportional to the energy deposited. Because the output is proportional, these detectors can tell energy, charge and type as a Geiger tube cannot.

concepts.name: Solid-state detector
concepts.statement: A semiconductor built to conduct only when ionization frees charge in it acts like a solid Geiger tube, and because it is solid it stops radiation in a short distance and misses few particles. The current is closely related to the energy deposited, so these detectors give sophisticated information as scintillators do.

concepts.name: Radiation detector
concepts.statement: A radiation detector is a device that detects and tracks the radiation from radioactive decay, directly or indirectly through the ionization it creates.

concepts.name: Scintillator
concepts.statement: A scintillator is a radiation detector that records the light produced when radiation interacts with its material.

concepts.name: Photomultiplier
concepts.statement: A photomultiplier is a device that converts light into an electrical signal by multiplying the photoelectrons a flash produces.

concepts.name: Nucleons
concepts.statement: Nucleons are the particles found inside nuclei, the positive proton and the neutral neutron, with nearly the same mass and both far heavier than an electron.

concepts.name: Unified atomic mass unit
concepts.statement: The unified atomic mass unit is defined so that a neutral $^{12}$C atom has a mass of exactly 12 u, and $1\;\text{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg $= 931.5$ MeV/$c^{2}$. A mass in MeV/$c^{2}$ becomes an energy in MeV when multiplied by $c^{2}$.

concepts.name: Writing a nuclide
concepts.statement: A nuclide is written ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N}$, with the mass number $A$ above, the atomic number $Z$ below, the element symbol, and the neutron number $N$ after it, and with $A = N + Z$ any one of these can be found from the others.

concepts.name: Isotopes
concepts.statement: Isotopes are nuclei with the same $Z$ and different $N$, such as hydrogen, deuterium and tritium. Their chemistry follows $Z$, while their mass and stability follow the whole nucleus.

concepts.name: Nuclear radius
concepts.statement: The radius of a nucleus is $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2$ fm, so its volume is proportional to the number of nucleons $A$. This is what happens if nucleons are packed so closely that there is no empty space between them.

concepts.name: Finding nuclear density
concepts.statement: The density of nuclear matter is found from $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$ and a mass of $A$ u; every nucleus has about the same density, about $2 \times 10^{14}$ times that of water.

concepts.name: Strong and weak nuclear forces
concepts.statement: Two forces act in the nucleus beside the Coulomb force: the strong nuclear force, about 100 times more attractive than the electromagnetic repulsion between protons but falling to zero within a few fm, and the weak nuclear force. Their strength is why nuclear decay energies are so large.

concepts.name: Chart of the nuclides
concepts.statement: The chart of the nuclides plots every known nuclide by $N$ against $Z$. Stable nuclei lie near $N = Z$ for light nuclei and with progressively more neutrons than protons for heavier ones, and nuclei off this band decay toward it.

concepts.name: Magic numbers
concepts.statement: Nuclei with certain numbers of protons or neutrons, the magic numbers, are unusually stable, which means the nucleus has shells as the atom does and closed shells are more stable.

concepts.name: Nucleus
concepts.statement: The nucleus is the region at the center of an atom, consisting of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Neutron
concepts.statement: A neutron is a neutral particle found in the nucleus, with nearly the same mass as a proton.

concepts.name: Nuclide
concepts.statement: A nuclide is a type of atom whose nucleus has specific numbers of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Mass number
concepts.statement: The mass number $A$ is the number of nucleons in a nucleus, the sum of its neutron number $N$ and its atomic number $Z$.

concepts.name: Neutron number
concepts.statement: The neutron number $N$ is the number of neutrons in a nucleus.

concepts.name: Atomic mass
concepts.statement: The atomic mass is the total mass of the protons, neutrons and electrons in a single atom.

concepts.name: Parent and daughter nuclides
concepts.statement: A decay turns a parent nuclide into a daughter, and a daughter may itself be unstable, so some parents start a whole series of decays that ends only at a stable nuclide, as the $^{238}$U series ends at $^{206}$Pb.

concepts.name: Writing an alpha decay equation
concepts.statement: An $\alpha$ decay equation is written by removing a $^{4}$He nucleus from the parent, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y}_{N-2} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}_{2}$: the daughter is the element two places lower in the periodic table, with a mass number four smaller.

concepts.name: Energy of a nuclear reaction
concepts.statement: The energy released in a nuclear reaction comes from the mass destroyed in it, $E = (\Delta m)c^{2}$. When the products have less total mass than the parent, the reaction releases energy and can happen spontaneously; when they have more, it needs an input of energy.

concepts.name: Finding a decay energy
concepts.statement: A decay energy is found from the atomic masses in the tables, which are those of neutral atoms, so the electrons must be counted. In $\alpha$ and $\beta^{-}$ decay they balance and the atomic masses can be subtracted directly; in $\beta^{+}$ decay two electron masses must also be subtracted.

concepts.name: Beta minus decay and the neutrino
concepts.statement: In $\beta^{-}$ decay a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton, and the nucleus creates and emits an electron and an electron’s antineutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y}_{N-1} + \beta^{-} + \bar{\nu}_{e}$. Without the antineutrino, energy, linear momentum and angular momentum would not be conserved.

concepts.name: Beta plus decay and electron capture
concepts.statement: Nuclei with too many protons for stability lower $Z$ by one, either by emitting a positron and an electron’s neutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y}_{N+1} + \beta^{+} + \nu_{e}$, or by capturing one of their own inner electrons. The two have the same effect on the nucleus.

concepts.name: Conservation of electron family number
terms: conservation of total electron family number
concepts.statement: The total number of members of the electron family is constant: electrons and electron’s neutrinos count $+1$ and their antimatter partners count $-1$, so an electron can never be created without an antimatter family member.

concepts.name: Conservation of nucleon number
concepts.statement: In every decay the total number of nucleons $A$ is the same before and after, even when protons turn into neutrons or the reverse, and the total charge is conserved as always.

concepts.name: Gamma decay
concepts.statement: In $\gamma$ decay a nucleus left in an excited state falls to lower levels by emitting photons, as an excited atom does, but with MeV energies. $\gamma$ decay does not change the nuclide.

concepts.name: Parent
concepts.statement: The parent is the original nucleus before a decay.

concepts.name: Daughter
concepts.statement: The daughter is the nucleus produced when a parent nucleus decays.

concepts.name: Decay
concepts.statement: Decay is the process by which the nucleus of an unstable atom loses mass and energy by emitting radiation.

concepts.name: Alpha decay
concepts.statement: Alpha decay is the type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits an alpha particle, a $^{4}$He nucleus.

concepts.name: Beta decay
concepts.statement: Beta decay is the type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits a beta particle, an electron or a positron.

concepts.name: Positron
